Sandy: English short form of Alexander or Sandra, from Greek 'defender of men'. Also used on its own as a unisex name.
Jitse: Frisian form of Justus, from Latin 'just, righteous'. Related forms are Joost and Just.
Lamia: Arabic, meaning 'shining' or 'radiant'. In Greek myth Lamia was a queen turned into a monster, but the Arabic name is unrelated.
Jessie: English, originally a Scottish pet form of Janet or Jean, now also from Jesse, Hebrew 'gift' or 'wealthy'. Used for girls and boys.
Tarik: Arabic Tariq, meaning 'morning star' or 'he who knocks at the door'. Also common in Turkish and Bosnian.
Tiziana: Italian feminine of Tiziano, from Latin Titianus, a Roman family name of uncertain meaning, perhaps linked to Titus.
Houda: Arabic Huda, meaning 'right guidance'. Popular among Belgian families of Moroccan origin.
Peter: Greek Petros, 'rock' or 'stone'. The apostle Simon was named Peter by Jesus; common across Europe.
Chaima: Arabic Shaima or Shaymaa, meaning 'one with a beauty mark'. Also the name of the Prophet's foster sister.
Lorenz: German form of Laurentius, from Latin 'from Laurentum' or 'laurel-crowned'. Related to Lawrence and Laurent.
Emeric: French form of Germanic Emmerich, from heimi 'home' and rik 'ruler'. Hungarian Imre is the same name.
Janelle: Modern English and American coinage, a feminine elaboration of Jane, from Hebrew 'God is gracious'.
Oumayma: Arabic Umayma, a diminutive of umm 'mother' or 'little mother'. Borne by a Companion of the Prophet.
Jaimy: Modern Dutch spelling of Jamie, a Scottish form of James, from Hebrew Yaakov, usually 'supplanter'.
Isabeau: Old French form of Isabel, itself from Elisabeth, Hebrew 'my God is an oath'. Sometimes also a Flemish variant.
Sammy: English pet form of Samuel or Samantha. Samuel is Hebrew, 'God has heard' or 'name of God'.
Aidan: Anglicised Irish Aodhán, a diminutive of Aodh, 'fire'. Borne by the Irish saint Aidan of Lindisfarne.
Salima: Arabic, feminine of Salim, meaning 'safe, healthy, sound'. Related to salam 'peace'.
Berkay: Turkish, from berk 'solid, firm' and kay 'to flow' or 'solid, strong'. A modern male name.
Brayan: Spelling variant of Brian, probably Celtic and linked to 'high' or 'noble'. Popular in Spanish-speaking communities.
Jihane: Arabic Jihan, 'world' or 'universe', of Persian origin (jahan). Used in Maghrebi families.
Maissa: Arabic Maysa, meaning 'proud, graceful stride'. Also a name of a type of tree in Arabic.
Murat: Turkish form of Arabic Murad, meaning 'desired, wished for'. Borne by several Ottoman sultans.
Ciara: Irish, feminine of Ciar, 'dark' or 'black-haired'. Also used as an Italian variant of Chiara, 'clear, bright'.
Egon: German, from Germanic ek or agi 'edge, sword point'. Also used in Dutch-speaking regions.
Mariem: Arabic form of Maryam, Mary. Ultimately Hebrew Miriam, of uncertain meaning, perhaps 'beloved' or 'bitter'.
Jean-Baptiste: French compound of Jean (John, Hebrew 'God is gracious') and Baptiste, 'the baptizer', after John the Baptist.
Daisy: English flower name, from 'day's eye'. Also used as a pet name for Margaret.
Loucas: French form of Lucas, from Greek Loukas, 'man from Lucania' or 'light'. Related to Luke.
Sid: English short form of Sidney or Siddharth. Sidney probably derives from 'wide island' or from Saint-Denis.
Estéban: Spanish and French variant of Esteban, from Greek Stephanos, 'crown' or 'wreath'. Related to Stephen.
Florentin: French and Romanian form of Latin Florentinus, 'blooming' or 'from Florence'. Related to Florence.
Hilal: Arabic, meaning 'crescent moon'. Used for both sexes, especially in Turkish and Arabic communities.
Maelys: Modern Breton-style name, probably a blend of Maël, 'prince' in Celtic, with names like Élise. Origin partly uncertain.
Manar: Arabic, meaning 'lighthouse' or 'beacon'. Used for girls and sometimes boys.
Romina: Italian and Spanish, probably from Latin Romanus 'Roman' or from Rome. Sometimes a form of Romy.
Samuël: Hebrew Shemuel, 'God has heard' or 'name of God'. The biblical prophet and judge.
Feyza: Turkish, from Arabic fayd, meaning 'abundance, plenty' or 'grace'. A feminine name.
Philip: Greek Philippos, 'lover of horses', from philos and hippos. One of the twelve apostles.
Ihsane: Arabic Ihsan, meaning 'excellence, doing good, charity'. Usually a boys' name; as a girls' name mainly in Morocco.
Mélodie: French, from Greek melodia 'singing a song'. A modern name inspired by music.
Calvin: From French Cauvin, a diminutive of chauve 'bald'. Best known through the reformer John Calvin.
Stefano: Italian form of Stephen, from Greek Stephanos, 'crown' or 'garland'.
Mourad: Arabic Murad, meaning 'desired, wished for'. The Maghrebi spelling of Murat.
Nika: Slavic short form of Veronika or Nikola, or from Greek nike 'victory'. Also Georgian and Japanese uses.
Enrico: Italian form of Henry, from Germanic heimi 'home' and rik 'ruler'.
Dalila: Arabic and Spanish form of Delilah. Arabic dalil means 'guide' or 'proof'; the biblical name is Hebrew, possibly 'delicate'.
Derya: Turkish, meaning 'sea' or 'ocean', from Persian darya.
Anita: Spanish and Italian diminutive of Ana, from Hebrew Hannah, 'grace, favour'. Also used in India.
Cem: Turkish, from Persian Jam or Jamshid, a legendary king; also associated with 'gathering' or 'ruler'. Borne by an Ottoman prince.
Mary: English form of Mary, Greek Maria from Hebrew Miriam. Meaning uncertain, perhaps 'beloved' or 'bitter'.
Joline: Probably an English or French blend of Jo with the -line ending, as in Caroline. Possibly also a form of Jolene. Origin uncertain.
Anil: Sanskrit, 'wind' or 'air'; also a Turkish name from anıl 'remembrance'. Used in both cultures.
Moreno: Italian and Spanish, meaning 'dark-skinned' or 'brown-haired'. Originally a nickname.
Nancy: English pet form of Ann or Agnes, ultimately from Hebrew Hannah 'grace' or Greek 'pure'.
Joaquin: Spanish form of Joachim, from Hebrew 'God will establish'. Traditionally the father of Mary.
Malcolm: Scottish, from Gaelic Máel Coluim, 'devotee of Saint Columba'. Borne by several Scottish kings.
Douwe: Frisian, from Germanic dau, probably 'dew' or related to Dutch names like Dauwe. Origin is uncertain.
Lenzo: Probably a short form of Lorenzo, Italian for Laurence, 'from Laurentum' or 'laurel'. Also related to Lenz.
Kay: Short form of Kai, Katharina or Kaj. Used in Dutch and German; also an Arthurian knight name, from Latin Caius.
Leroy: French, from le roi, 'the king'. Originally a nickname for a royal servant or one who played the king.
Asmaa: Arabic Asma, meaning 'more elevated, loftier' or 'excellent'. Name of a Companion of the Prophet.
Baptist: Dutch form of Baptiste, from Greek baptistes, 'one who baptizes'. After John the Baptist.
Moïse: French form of Moses, from Hebrew Moshe, possibly 'drawn out' or related to Egyptian 'son'.
Emmanuella: Feminine of Emmanuel, Hebrew 'God is with us'. Variant spelling of Emanuela.
Merijn: Dutch form of Merlin, from Welsh Myrddin, possibly 'sea fortress'. The Arthurian wizard.
Calista: Greek, from kallistos, 'most beautiful'. Also a Greek mythological nymph.
Tyana: Probably a modern coinage, perhaps from the ancient city of Tyana or a blend of Tia and Ana. Origin uncertain.
Koray: Turkish, from kor 'ember' and ay 'moon', meaning 'glowing ember'. A modern male name.
Largo: Probably from Italian or Spanish largo, 'wide, broad', also a musical tempo term. Rare as a first name; origin uncertain.
Saïd: Arabic Said, meaning 'happy, fortunate'. Common among Muslim families.
Francisco: Spanish and Portuguese form of Francis, from Latin Franciscus, 'Frenchman' or 'free man'.
Nohan: Modern name, probably from Noah combined with the Breton -han ending. Origin uncertain.
Dikra: Arabic Dhikra, meaning 'remembrance, memory'. Also used in Moroccan families.
Zeliha: Turkish, from Arabic Zulaykha, the biblical Potiphar's wife in Islamic tradition. Possibly 'bright, shining'.
Zinedine: Arabic Zayn al-Din, 'ornament of the faith'. Widely known through footballer Zinedine Zidane.
Kaya: Multiple origins: Japanese 'rest', Turkish 'rock', Hopi 'wise child'. Also a Polish form of Kaja.
Thiebe: Flemish, probably a form of Thijs or Theobald, from Germanic theud 'people' and bald 'bold'. Origin uncertain.
Fatima-Zahra: Arabic. Fatima means 'one who abstains' and Zahra 'radiant, shining'. Both are titles of the Prophet's daughter.
Yvan: French and Slavic form of Ivan, from John, Hebrew 'God is gracious'.
Athina: Greek form of Athena, the goddess of wisdom. Also the Greek name of the city Athens.
Destiny: English word name meaning 'fate, what is destined'. Used as a given name from the late 20th century.
Tayron: Modern variant of Tyron or Tyrone, from Irish Tír Eoghain, 'land of Eoghan'. Spelling probably influenced by Tyrone Power.
Elysa: Probably a variant of Elisa or Elysia, from Elisabeth, Hebrew 'my God is an oath'. Origin partly uncertain.
Metin: Turkish, meaning 'firm, solid, strong'. From Arabic matin.
Loic: Breton form of Louis, from Germanic Chlodovech, 'famous warrior'. Written Loïc in French.
Ombeline: French, from Latin umbella 'parasol' or from Germanic Amalberga. Origin uncertain.
Taylan: Turkish, probably from taylan 'a flowing movement' or Mongol-Turkic origin. Possibly also from Taylan 'brave'. Origin uncertain.
Shayna: Yiddish, from sheyn, 'beautiful'. Also Irish Sheena, a form of Jane.
Serhat: Turkish, from Arabic sarhad meaning 'border, frontier'. A male name.
Hélèna: French spelling of Helena, from Greek Helene, possibly 'torch' or 'shining light'.
Ingrid: Scandinavian, from Old Norse Ingi, a god of fertility, and fríðr 'beautiful'.
Mathew: Variant spelling of Matthew, from Hebrew Mattityahu, 'gift of God'.
Shaun: Anglicised spelling of Irish Seán, the Irish form of John, Hebrew 'God is gracious'.
Maelle: Breton, feminine of Maël, from Celtic 'prince' or 'chief'.
Abdurrahman: Arabic Abd al-Rahman, 'servant of the Most Merciful'. One of the most common Muslim names.
Inês: Portuguese form of Agnes, from Greek hagne 'pure' or Latin agnus 'lamb'.
Blessing: English word name, from 'to bless'. Common in Nigeria and Ghana.
Casey: Irish, from Ó Cathasaigh, 'descendant of Cathasach', meaning 'vigilant'. Used for both sexes.
Naïs: Provençal, a short form of Anaïs, itself from Greek Anna. Also Greek naias 'water nymph'.
Antoinette: French feminine diminutive of Antoine, from Roman Antonius, of uncertain meaning. Famous via Marie Antoinette.
Tars: Probably a short form of Tarsus or Tarsicius, or Dutch nickname. Rare; origin uncertain.
Nathaël: French form of Nathanael, Hebrew 'God has given'. Variant of Nathanaël.
Nida: Arabic, meaning 'call' or 'announcement'. Also a Lithuanian place name.
Vienna: From the Austrian capital, whose name derives from Celtic Vindobona. Modern given name.
Yakup: Turkish form of Jacob, from Hebrew Yaakov, usually 'supplanter' or 'may God protect'.
Camie: Probably a variant of Cammie or Camille, from Latin camillus, a young attendant at a sacrifice. Origin uncertain.
Aydan: Turkish, 'moonlike', from ay 'moon'. Also a variant of Aidan, Irish 'little fire'.
Anaël: French name of Hebrew origin, from the angel Anael, possibly 'grace of God'.
Neïla: Arabic Nayla, meaning 'one who attains' or 'achiever'. Common in North African families.
Hala: Arabic, meaning 'halo' or 'ring around the moon'. Also a Hawaiian pandanus tree name.
Scarlett: English, from the surname Scarlett, 'scarlet cloth' or a seller of it. Made famous by Gone with the Wind.
Marko: Slavic, Estonian and Finnish form of Mark, from Latin Marcus, possibly 'dedicated to Mars'.
Niklas: German and Scandinavian form of Nicholas, from Greek 'victory of the people'.
Lowiek: Probably a Flemish or Dutch variant of Lodewijk, Dutch for Louis, Germanic 'famous warrior'. Origin uncertain.
Rumeysa: Turkish form of Arabic Rumaysa, a name of a Companion of the Prophet, possibly 'fine-grained, graceful'.
Alesia: Probably a form of Alexia or the ancient Gaulish town Alesia. Also a Slavic variant of Alice. Origin uncertain.
Meliha: Turkish and Bosnian, from Arabic Maliha, 'beautiful, pretty'.
Konstantinos: Greek form of Constantine, from Latin constans, 'steadfast, constant'.
Rodayna: Arabic Rudayna, probably related to the 'lance' of Rudayna, a spear-maker. Rare; origin partly uncertain.
Lorin: Probably a variant of Lauren or Lorraine, or Romanian male Lorin from Laurentiu. Origin uncertain.
Mayssane: Arabic Maysan, derived from maysan, meaning 'proud walk' or 'graceful stride'. Alternative spelling of Maissa.
Greta: Short form of Margareta, from Greek margarites, 'pearl'. Common in Germanic and Baltic regions.
Marie-Louise: French compound of Marie (Hebrew Miriam) and Louise (feminine of Louis, 'famous warrior').
Nermine: Arabic, from Persian nesrin, 'wild rose' or 'dog rose'. Common in Egypt.
Honorine: French, from Latin Honorina, 'honour'. A feminine of Honoré.
Louic: Variant of Loïc or Loïs, from Louis, Germanic 'famous warrior'. Origin partly uncertain.
Alexe: French short form of Alexandre or Alexandra, from Greek 'defender of men'. Used on its own in recent years.
Emanuela: Italian feminine of Emanuele, Hebrew Immanuel, 'God is with us'.
Mali: Probably Thai 'jasmine' or Welsh short form of Mary. Also a West African country. Origin varies.
Moritz: German form of Maurice, from Latin Mauritius, 'dark-skinned, Moorish'.
Abou: Arabic abu, 'father of', used as a name element in West African and Maghrebi families. Often short for names like Aboubakar.
Myron: Greek, from myron, 'sweet oil' or 'perfume'. Borne by an ancient Greek sculptor.
Agnes: Greek, from hagne 'pure', later associated with Latin agnus 'lamb'. A Roman martyr saint.
Bintou: West African, from Arabic bint, 'daughter'. Used among Mandinka and Fula peoples.
Jaber: Arabic Jabir, meaning 'comforter' or 'one who mends'. Name of several Companions of the Prophet.
Jet: Dutch, a short form of Henriette or Jetty. Also the English word for black gemstone.
Leontine: French, feminine of Leontin, from Latin leo, 'lion'.
Miryam: Variant spelling of Miriam, the Hebrew name of Moses' sister. Meaning uncertain, perhaps 'beloved' or 'bitter'.
Damaris: Greek, possibly meaning 'heifer' or 'gentle'. Biblical name of an Athenian woman converted by Paul.
Quin: Probably short for Quinn, from Irish Ó Cuinn 'descendant of Conn', meaning 'wisdom'. Dutch usage also from Quinten.
Simona: Italian, Czech and Romanian feminine of Simon, from Hebrew 'he has heard'.
Conrad: Germanic, from kuoni 'brave' and rat 'counsel'. Popular in German and English use.
Piotr: Polish and Russian form of Peter, from Greek petros, 'rock'.
Houdaifa: Arabic Hudhayfa, possibly 'little wolf' or from hadhf 'to cut off'. Name of a Companion of the Prophet.
Pharell: Variant spelling of Pharrell, probably after Pharrell Williams. The name's origin is uncertain, possibly from Irish Farrell 'valour'.
Ron: English short form of Ronald, from Old Norse Rögnvaldr 'ruler's counsel'. Also Hebrew ron, 'song, joy'.
Wasim: Arabic, meaning 'handsome, graceful' or 'of good looks'.
Lyan: Modern name, probably a form of Lian or Ryan, or Hebrew-style Lian. Origin uncertain.
Darya: Persian and Slavic. Persian darya means 'sea'; Russian Darya is a form of Daria, 'possessing goodness'.
Nathalia: Latinised form of Natalia, from Latin natalis, 'born at Christmas'.
Samar: Arabic, 'evening conversation' or 'fruits' (Hindi). A girls' name in Arabic usage.
Katerina: Slavic and Greek form of Katherine, from Greek aikaterine, perhaps 'pure'.
Rokaya: Arabic Ruqayya, meaning 'charm, spell' or 'she who rises'. Name of a daughter of the Prophet.
Elysia: Latinate, from the Elysian Fields, the paradise of Greek myth. A modern given name.
Harrison: English surname turned given name, 'son of Harry', where Harry is a form of Henry.
Ipek: Turkish, spelt İpek, meaning 'silk'. A common girls' name in Turkey.
Lester: English surname from Leicester. The city name derives from Old English, with an uncertain first element.
Matty: English pet form of Matthew or Martha, from Hebrew 'gift of God'.
Spencer: English occupational surname meaning 'dispenser of provisions', from Old French despensier.
Alihan: Turkish compound of Ali, Arabic 'exalted', and han, 'ruler, khan'.
Ardian: Albanian, from Ardi 'to arrive' or Illyrian Ardian, perhaps 'of the Adriatic'. Origin partly uncertain.
Bryce: Scottish surname, probably from Brice, possibly Celtic 'speckled' or Gaulish. Origin uncertain.
Harald: Scandinavian, from Old Norse Haraldr, 'army ruler' (harja and valdr).
Petra: Feminine of Peter, from Greek petra, 'rock'. Also a Jordanian ancient city.
Rivka: Hebrew form of Rebecca, from the biblical wife of Isaac. Possibly meaning 'to bind' or 'noose'.
Frie: Dutch and Flemish short form of Alfrida or Friederike, from Germanic frid, 'peace'. Also a Frisian-style short form.
Julio: Spanish and Portuguese form of Julius, a Roman family name, perhaps from 'youthful' or Jove.
Loewis: Variant of Lewis, English form of Louis, from Germanic 'famous warrior'.
Maely: Modern variant of Maëlys or Maëlle, from Breton Maël, 'prince'.
Moustafa: Arabic Mustafa, meaning 'chosen, selected'. An epithet of the Prophet Muhammad.
Narek: Armenian, after the monastery of Narek and the poet Grigor Narekatsi. Probably 'of the Narek river'. Origin partly uncertain.
Aitana: Spanish, from a mountain in Alicante, Sierra Aitana. Possibly of pre-Roman origin; meaning uncertain.
Allegra: Italian, meaning 'cheerful' or 'lively'. Also a musical tempo term.
Khloé: Spelling of Chloe, from Greek khloe, 'young green shoot'. An epithet of the goddess Demeter.
Martim: Portuguese form of Martin, from Latin Martinus, 'of Mars'.
Maélie: French modern name, from Breton Maël 'prince', possibly blended with names such as Amélie.
Abu: Arabic, 'father of'. Used as a first name in parts of Africa and South Asia.
Aléandro: Possibly an altered form of Alejandro or Leandro, from Greek 'defender of men' or 'lion man'. Origin uncertain.
Heavenly: English word name, from 'of heaven'. A modern coinage as a girl's name.
Houdeyfa: Arabic Hudhayfa, perhaps 'little wolf'. A variant of Houdaifa.
Giusy: Italian, a pet form of Giuseppina or Giuseppa, from Hebrew Yosef, 'he will add'.
Elmo: Italian short form of Erasmus, 'beloved', or from Germanic helm 'helmet, protection'. Also a saint, Elmo.
Enver: Turkish and Albanian, from Arabic Anwar, 'more luminous, brighter'.
Irma: Germanic short form of names starting with irmin, 'whole, universal'. Also a Finnish and Spanish name.
Trixie: English pet form of Beatrix, from Latin 'she who brings joy' or 'voyager'.
Yarah: Probably Arabic Yara, 'small butterfly' or 'little bee', or from Hebrew Yara. Origin varies.
Felipe: Spanish and Portuguese form of Philip, from Greek 'lover of horses'.
Noya: Hebrew, meaning 'beauty' or 'ornament of God'. Used in modern Israel.
Saran: Probably a Thai or Indian name, or a variant of Sara. Origin uncertain.
Aura: Latin and Greek, 'breeze' or 'gentle wind'. Also Spanish and Romanian name from Latin 'gold'.
Adea: Albanian modern name, possibly from Illyrian roots. Origin uncertain.
Isabela: Spanish and Portuguese form of Isabel, from Elisabeth, Hebrew 'my God is an oath'.
Maybelle: English, probably from Mabel, a short form of Amabel, from Latin amabilis 'lovable'. Influenced by French belle.
Saona: Probably from the Dominican island Saona, or an invented name. Origin uncertain.
Sevda: Turkish, from Arabic sawda, 'love, passion'. A girls' name in Turkey and Azerbaijan.
Skyler: English form of Dutch Schuyler, 'scholar' or 'shelter'. Now popular as a unisex name.
Aleks: Short form of Aleksander or Aleksandr, from Greek 'defender of men'.
Loulou: French pet name, a reduplicated form of Louise or Louis. Also French 'wolf cub'.
Octavie: French feminine of Octave, from Latin octavus, 'eighth'.
Pip: English pet form of Philip or Pippa, or from Dickens's Great Expectations. Philip means 'lover of horses'.
Izabela: Polish, Portuguese and Czech form of Isabel, from Elisabeth, Hebrew 'my God is an oath'.
Letty: English pet form of Letitia, from Latin laetitia, 'joy'. Also from Lettice.
Menachem: Hebrew, meaning 'comforter'. Common in Jewish communities, notably the Antwerp Hasidim.
